clinicalPearls: Visible yellow discolouration of skin and sclerae from raised serum bilirubin, extremely common in newborns and usually due to unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinaemia.
Physiological jaundice appears after the first 24 hours, peaks around days 3-5 in term infants, and resolves without harm; it reflects normal neonatal bilirubin handling.
Jaundice in the first 24 hours of life is always pathological and demands urgent evaluation, commonly for haemolysis.
Key pathological causes include blood-group incompatibility (Rh, ABO), G6PD deficiency, sepsis, and other haemolytic conditions.
Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinaemia is never physiological and requires investigation for cholestasis, notably biliary atresia, which needs early surgery.
Breastfeeding-associated (early, from inadequate intake) and breast-milk (later, prolonged) jaundice are common benign patterns once other causes are excluded.
Management depends on bilirubin level plotted against age in hours and risk factors; phototherapy is first-line and exchange transfusion is reserved for dangerously high or rapidly rising levels.
The feared complication is bilirubin-induced neurological dysfunction (acute encephalopathy progressing to kernicterus), which is preventable with timely treatment.
reference.pathophysiology: Newborns have increased bilirubin production from a high red cell mass with shorter red cell lifespan, combined with immature hepatic conjugation (low UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity) and enhanced enterohepatic recirculation of bilirubin. These factors produce transient physiological unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Pathological jaundice arises when production is excessive (haemolysis, extravasated blood), conjugation or uptake is impaired, or excretion is obstructed (cholestasis). Unbound unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and can cross the blood-brain barrier, depositing in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei to cause neurotoxicity.
additionalDifferentials: G6PD deficiency and other red cell enzyme/membrane defects
Biliary atresia and other causes of neonatal cholestasis
additionalInvestigations: Total and conjugated (direct) serum bilirubin, interpreted against age in hours
Blood group and direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test on infant and mother
Full blood count, reticulocyte count, and blood film
Thyroid function and septic screen when suggested by the picture
Assessment for cholestasis (e.g. pale stools, dark urine) when direct bilirubin is raised
redFlags: Jaundice within the first 24 hours of life
Rapidly rising bilirubin or a level near the exchange-transfusion threshold
Signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy: lethargy, poor feeding, hypotonia progressing to hypertonia, high-pitched cry, arching
Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, pale stools, and dark urine suggesting biliary atresia
Prolonged jaundice beyond two weeks (term) or three weeks (preterm) requiring evaluation
reference.prognosis: Most neonatal jaundice is benign and resolves without sequelae; with appropriate monitoring and treatment, kernicterus is largely preventable, but untreated severe hyperbilirubinaemia can cause permanent neurological injury.
pitfalls: Dismissing jaundice in the first 24 hours as physiological
Failing to fractionate bilirubin and missing cholestasis / biliary atresia
Assessing jaundice by clinical appearance alone rather than measured bilirubin against age-specific thresholds
Overlooking dehydration from inadequate feeding as a contributor in early breastfeeding jaundice
Not investigating jaundice that persists beyond the expected period
management: Treat significant unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with phototherapy, interpreting levels against age-in-hours thresholds
Perform exchange transfusion for severe or rapidly rising bilirubin or signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy
Give intravenous immunoglobulin in isoimmune haemolytic disease (Rh or ABO) to reduce haemolysis and the need for exchange transfusion
Ensure adequate feeding and hydration, supporting breastfeeding and correcting inadequate intake
Investigate and treat the underlying cause, including antibiotics for sepsis and early surgical referral (Kasai portoenterostomy) for biliary atresia in conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
Monitor bilirubin trends and watch for evolving neurological signs to prevent kernicterus
